claim: The RNA polymerase II largest subunit (Rpb1) contains a unique C-terminal domain (CTD) that plays multiple roles during transcription.
source: The RNA polymerase II largest subunit (Rpb1) contains a unique C-terminal domain (CTD) that plays multiple roles during transcription.
evidence: This is a general statement about Rpb1 CTD function, supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: The CTD is composed of consensus Y1S2P3T4S5P6S7 repeats.
source: The CTD is composed of consensus Y1S2P3T4S5P6S7 repeats, in which Ser, Thr and Tyr residues can all be phosphorylated.
evidence: This describes the known consensus sequence of the CTD, which is established knowledge.

claim: Ser, Thr and Tyr residues in the CTD can all be phosphorylated.
source: The CTD is composed of consensus Y1S2P3T4S5P6S7 repeats, in which Ser, Thr and Tyr residues can all be phosphorylated.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and citations in the field.

claim: Cells expressing an Rpb1 derivative with all Tyr residues mutated to Phe (Rpb1-Y1F) were inviable.
source: Cells expressing an Rpb1 derivative with all Tyr residues mutated to Phe (Rpb1-Y1F) were inviable.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from complementation tests shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Rpb1-Y1F was unstable and degraded to a CTD-less form.
source: Remarkably, Rpb1-Y1F was unstable, degraded to a CTD-less form
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Rpb1-Y1F stability was fully rescued by restoration of a single C-terminal Tyr (Rpb1-25F+Y).
source: however stability, but not cell viability, was fully rescued by restoration of a single C-terminal Tyr (Rpb1-25F+Y).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Cell viability was not rescued by restoration of a single C-terminal Tyr (Rpb1-25F+Y).
source: however stability, but not cell viability, was fully rescued by restoration of a single C-terminal Tyr (Rpb1-25F+Y).
evidence: This is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Cytoplasmic and nucleoplasmic Rpb1 was phosphorylated exclusively on Tyr1.
source: Cytoplasmic and nucleoplasmic Rpb1 was phosphorylated exclusively on Tyr1
evidence: This is supported by subcellular fractionation and Western blot data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Phosphorylation specifically of Tyr1 prevented CTD degradation by the proteasome in vitro.
source: and phosphorylation specifically of Tyr1 prevented CTD degradation by the proteasome in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro proteasome assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Tyr1 phosphorylation was detected on chromatin-associated, hyperphosphorylated Rpb1.
source: Tyr1 phosphorylation was also detected on chromatin-associated, hyperphosphorylated Rpb1, consistent with a role in transcription.
evidence: This is supported by subcellular fractionation data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Tyr1 phosphorylation plays a role in transcription.
source: Tyr1 phosphorylation was also detected on chromatin-associated, hyperphosphorylated Rpb1, consistent with a role in transcription.
evidence: This is inferred from the detection of Tyr1-P on chromatin-associated Rpb1 and the accumulation of uaRNAs in mutant cells.

claim: Upstream antisense (ua) RNAs accumulated in Rpb1-25F+Y cells.
source: Indeed, we detected accumulation of upstream antisense (ua) RNAs in Rpb1-25F+Y cells, indicating a role for Tyr1 in uaRNA expression.
evidence: This is supported by 3'READS sequencing data shown in Figure 4B and RT-qPCR validation in Figure 4C.

claim: Tyr1 plays a role in uaRNA expression.
source: Indeed, we detected accumulation of upstream antisense (ua) RNAs in Rpb1-25F+Y cells, indicating a role for Tyr1 in uaRNA expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the accumulation of uaRNAs in Rpb1-25F+Y cells.

claim: RNA polymerase II (RNAP II) is a multisubunit enzyme responsible in eukaryotes for transcription of all mRNAs and many non-coding RNAs.
source: RNA polymerase II (RNAP II) is a multisubunit enzyme responsible in eukaryotes for transcription of all mRNAs and many non-coding RNAs.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about RNAP II function.

claim: The CTD is composed of up to 52 heptad repeats with the consensus sequence Tyr1-Ser2-Pro3-Thr4-Ser5-Pro6-Ser7 (YSPTSPS).
source: Rpb1, the largest subunit, contains a unique C-terminal domain (CTD), composed of up to 52 heptad repeats with the consensus sequence Tyr1-Ser2-Pro3-Thr4-Ser5-Pro6-Ser7 (YSPTSPS).
evidence: This is established knowledge about CTD structure.

claim: The CTD performs multiple functions during transcription.
source: The CTD performs multiple functions during transcription (Buratowski, 2009; Munoz et al., 2010; Egloff et al., 2012; Hsin and Manley, 2012; Heidemann et al., 2013), most of which are dependent on phosphorylation of specific CTD residues.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Most CTD functions are dependent on phosphorylation of specific CTD residues.
source: The CTD performs multiple functions during transcription (Buratowski, 2009; Munoz et al., 2010; Egloff et al., 2012; Hsin and Manley, 2012; Heidemann et al., 2013), most of which are dependent on phosphorylation of specific CTD residues.
evidence: This is supported by citations and established knowledge.

claim: Ser5 phosphorylation promotes recruitment of capping enzyme.
source: For example, Ser5 phosphorylation (Ser5-P) promotes recruitment of capping enzyme (Fabrega et al., 2003)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fabrega et al., 2003.

claim: Ser2-P can be important for 3′ mRNA processing.
source: and Ser2-P can be important for 3′ mRNA processing (Kim et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kim et al., 2004.

claim: Ser7-P functions in 3′ processing of snRNAs.
source: Ser7-P and Thr4-P also function in 3′ processing, of snRNAs (Egloff et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Egloff et al., 2007.

claim: Thr4-P functions in 3′ processing of histone mRNAs.
source: and histone mRNAs (Hsin et al., 2011), respectively
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hsin et al., 2011.

claim: Thr4-P functions in transcription elongation.
source: with the later also functioning in transcription elongation (Hintermair et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hintermair et al., 2012.

claim: Tyr1 can be phosphorylated in mammals by c-Abl.
source: Tyr1 can be phosphorylated in mammals (by c-Abl; Baskaran et al., 1993)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Baskaran et al., 1993.

claim: Tyr1 can be phosphorylated in yeast.
source: and yeast (Mayer et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mayer et al., 2012.

claim: In yeast, Tyr1 phosphorylation may prevent premature recruitment of termination factors.
source: where it may prevent premature recruitment of termination factors.
evidence: This is speculative, based on prior work in yeast.

claim: The function(s) of Tyr1 and Tyr1-P in metazoans are unknown.
source: However, the function(s) of Tyr1 and Tyr1-P in metazoans are unknown.
evidence: This statement indicates a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: An Rpb1 derivative containing a CTD with 26 YSPTSPS repeats (Rpb1-26r) plus the ten C-terminal non-consensus residues confers cell viability.
source: We showed that an Rpb1 derivative containing a CTD with 26 YSPTSPS repeats (Rpb1-26r) plus the ten C-terminal non-consensus residues, important for stability (Chapman et al., 2005), confers cell viability
evidence: This is supported by prior work from the authors and citation to Chapman et al., 2005.

claim: The ten C-terminal non-consensus residues are important for stability.
source: plus the ten C-terminal non-consensus residues, important for stability (Chapman et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chapman et al., 2005.

claim: A comparable Rpb1 derivative with all Thr4 residues changed to Val was inviable.
source: while a comparable derivative with all Thr4 residues changed to Val was inviable (Hsin et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work by Hsin et al., 2011.

claim: Tyr1 was suggested to be essential for viability in S. cerevisiae.
source: Tyr1 was suggested to be essential for viability in S. cerevisiae (West and Corden, 1995)
evidence: This is supported by citation to West and Corden, 1995.

claim: Tyr1 is not essential for viability in S. pombe.
source: but not in S. pombe (Schwer and Shuman, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schwer and Shuman, 2011.

claim: Rpb1-Y1F was unable to complement Rpb1.
source: Rpb1-Y1F was unable to complement Rpb1, whereas Rpb1-26r fully restored viability (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by complementation assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Rpb1-26r fully restored viability.
source: Rpb1-Y1F was unable to complement Rpb1, whereas Rpb1-26r fully restored viability (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by complementation assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Cells expressing Rpb1-Y1F (Y1F) stopped growing around 24 hr in medium containing tet.
source: Cells expressing Rpb1-Y1F (Y1F) stopped growing around 24 hr in medium containing tet (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Rpb1-Y1F levels were significantly reduced compared to Rpb1-26r.
source: Rpb1-Y1F levels were indeed significantly reduced compared to Rpb1-26r (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: A lower molecular weight form of Rpb1-Y1F was observed in all Y1F cell lines.
source: Importantly, accumulation of a lower molecular weight form (indicated by *) was observed in all Y1F cell lines.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The lower molecular weight form of Rpb1-Y1F corresponds to a derivative likely precisely lacking the CTD.
source: This corresponds to a derivative likely precisely lacking the CTD, as it migrated slightly more rapidly than an Rpb1 derivative containing six heptads (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is inferred from the migration pattern on Western blot compared to a known standard.

claim: An Rpb1-Y1F derivative (20F+6Y) in which the F residues in the C-terminal six heptads were reverted to Y was completely stable.
source: We first analyzed an Rpb1-Y1F derivative (20F+6Y) in which the F residues in the C-terminal six heptads were reverted to Y, and found that this derivative was completely stable (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Cells expressing Rpb1-20F+6Y remained inviable.
source: although cells expressing Rpb1-20F+6Y remained inviable (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by complementation test data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: A single Tyr residue in the C terminal-most heptad was sufficient to prevent Rpb1 degradation.
source: Strikingly, this single Tyr residue was sufficient to prevent Rpb1 degradation, as the truncated isoform, which we denote Rpb1-b, was absent, and Rpb1-25F+Y levels were comparable to Rpb1-26r in multiple 25F+Y cell lines (Figure 1C; quantitation of the amount of degraded Rpb1 observed in multiple experiments is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1C and quantitation in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Despite the restoration of Rpb1 stability, 25F+Y cells remained inviable.
source: However, despite the restoration of Rpb1 stability, 25F+Y cells remained inviable (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Rpb1-25F+Y is Tyr1-phosphorylated in DT40 cells.
source: To address this, we utilized an anti-phospho-Tyr1 Ab (Mayer et al., 2012) to examine Tyr1 phosphorylation (Tyr1-P) of Rpb1-25F+Y and Rpb1-26r by WB; both proteins were indeed Tyr1-phosphorylated (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2A using an anti-phospho-Tyr1 antibody.

claim: Rpb1-26r is Tyr1-phosphorylated in DT40 cells.
source: To address this, we utilized an anti-phospho-Tyr1 Ab (Mayer et al., 2012) to examine Tyr1 phosphorylation (Tyr1-P) of Rpb1-25F+Y and Rpb1-26r by WB; both proteins were indeed Tyr1-phosphorylated (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2A using an anti-phospho-Tyr1 antibody.

claim: Rpb1-b was detected in all three fractions (cytoplasmic, nuclear, and chromatin-bound) from Y1F cells.
source: Rpb1-b (indicated by *) was detected in all three fractions from Y1F cells, but barely or not at all in the 26r fractions (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by subcellular fractionation and Western blot data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Rpb1-b was barely or not at all detected in the 26r fractions.
source: Rpb1-b (indicated by *) was detected in all three fractions from Y1F cells, but barely or not at all in the 26r fractions (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by subcellular fractionation and Western blot data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The relative (and absolute) Rpb1-b levels were lowest in the cytoplasm.
source: The relative (and absolute) Rpb1-b levels were lowest in the cytoplasm, while Rpb1-b was essentially the only form on Y1F chromatin.
evidence: This is inferred from the Western blot data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Rpb1-b was essentially the only form on Y1F chromatin.
source: The relative (and absolute) Rpb1-b levels were lowest in the cytoplasm, while Rpb1-b was essentially the only form on Y1F chromatin.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Rpb1-b was not detected in 25F+Y cell fractions.
source: As anticipated, Rpb1-b was not detected in 25F+Y cell fractions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by subcellular fractionation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Robust Tyr1-P was detected in all three fractions (cytoplasmic, nuclear, and chromatin-bound) in wild-type DT40 cells.
source: We next determined whether Tyr1-P could also be detected on Rpb1 in all three fractions, in this case using extracts from wild-type DT40 (Figure 2C) and human HEK293 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) cells. Robust Tyr1-P was indeed detected in all three fractions in both cell types.
evidence: This is supported by subcellular fractionation and Western blot data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Robust Tyr1-P was detected in all three fractions (cytoplasmic, nuclear, and chromatin-bound) in human HEK293 cells.
source: We next determined whether Tyr1-P could also be detected on Rpb1 in all three fractions, in this case using extracts from wild-type DT40 (Figure 2C) and human HEK293 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) cells. Robust Tyr1-P was indeed detected in all three fractions in both cell types.
evidence: This is supported by subcellular fractionation and Western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In both cytoplasm and nucleoplasm, Tyr1-P was observed only on hypophosphorylated Rpb1.
source: Notably, in both cytoplasm and nucleoplasm, Tyr1-P was observed only on hypophosphorylated Rpb1 (the lower band), while it was found primarily on the hyperphosphorylated isoform on chromatin.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Tyr1-P was found primarily on the hyperphosphorylated isoform on chromatin.
source: Notably, in both cytoplasm and nucleoplasm, Tyr1-P was observed only on hypophosphorylated Rpb1 (the lower band), while it was found primarily on the hyperphosphorylated isoform on chromatin.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: CTD phosphorylation is limited to Tyr1 in the cytoplasm and nucleoplasm.
source: This suggests both that CTD phosphorylation is limited to Tyr1 in the cytoplasm and nucleoplasm and that Tyr1-P is present on hyperphosphorylated RNAP II found on active genes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that only Tyr1-P is detected on hypophosphorylated Rpb1 in cytoplasm and nucleoplasm.

claim: Tyr1-P is present on hyperphosphorylated RNAP II found on active genes.
source: This suggests both that CTD phosphorylation is limited to Tyr1 in the cytoplasm and nucleoplasm and that Tyr1-P is present on hyperphosphorylated RNAP II found on active genes.
evidence: This is inferred from the detection of Tyr1-P on chromatin-associated hyperphosphorylated Rpb1.

claim: Phosphorylation on Ser 2, 5 and 7 and Thr4 were nearly undetectable in cytoplasmic and nuclear fractions.
source: We also examined phosphorylation on Ser 2, 5 and 7 and Thr4 (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B). All these modifications were nearly undetectable in cytoplasmic and nuclear fractions, present almost exclusively on chromatin-associated, hyperphosphorylated Rpb1.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Phosphorylation on Ser 2, 5 and 7 and Thr4 were present almost exclusively on chromatin-associated, hyperphosphorylated Rpb1.
source: We also examined phosphorylation on Ser 2, 5 and 7 and Thr4 (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B). All these modifications were nearly undetectable in cytoplasmic and nuclear fractions, present almost exclusively on chromatin-associated, hyperphosphorylated Rpb1.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Tyr1, and only Tyr1, is phosphorylated before RNAP II engages in transcription.
source: Together, our data show that Tyr1, and only Tyr1, is phosphorylated before RNAP II engages in transcription, and support the idea that Tyr1-P functions in stabilizing the CTD when RNAP II is not transcribing, and perhaps also plays a role during transcription.
evidence: This is inferred from the subcellular fractionation data showing Tyr1-P in cytoplasm and nucleoplasm but not other CTD phosphorylations.

claim: Tyr1-P functions in stabilizing the CTD when RNAP II is not transcribing.
source: Together, our data show that Tyr1, and only Tyr1, is phosphorylated before RNAP II engages in transcription, and support the idea that Tyr1-P functions in stabilizing the CTD when RNAP II is not transcribing, and perhaps also plays a role during transcription.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing Tyr1-P prevents CTD degradation and is present on non-chromatin-associated Rpb1.

claim: Tyr1-P perhaps also plays a role during transcription.
source: Together, our data show that Tyr1, and only Tyr1, is phosphorylated before RNAP II engages in transcription, and support the idea that Tyr1-P functions in stabilizing the CTD when RNAP II is not transcribing, and perhaps also plays a role during transcription.
evidence: This is speculative, based on the detection of Tyr1-P on chromatin-associated Rpb1.

claim: Tyr1-P was detected on Rpb1 immunoprecipitated by Abs recognizing Ser5-P and Ser2-P.
source: Consistent with this, Tyr1-P was detected on Rpb1 immunoprecipitated by Abs recognizing Ser5-P and Ser2-P (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation and Western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The proteasome has been shown to associate both with RNAP II and with active genes.
source: One possibility is that the CTD is degraded by the proteasome, which has been shown to associate both with RNAP II and with active genes (Gillette et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gillette et al., 2004.

claim: Certain naturally unstructured proteins can be degraded by the proteasome in a ubiquitin-independent manner.
source: Additionally, certain naturally unstructured proteins can be degraded by the proteasome in a ubiquitin-independent manner (Sheaff et al., 2000; Tofaris et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sheaff et al., 2000 and Tofaris et al., 2001.

claim: The CTD is considered a structure-less domain.
source: Since the CTD is considered a structure-less domain (Meinhart et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Meinhart et al., 2005.

claim: The CTD is a natural proteasome substrate.
source: we hypothesized that the CTD is a natural proteasome substrate, and that Tyr1-P prevents its proteasomal degradation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the unstructured nature of the CTD and prior knowledge about proteasome substrates.

claim: Tyr1-P prevents proteasomal degradation of the CTD.
source: we hypothesized that the CTD is a natural proteasome substrate, and that Tyr1-P prevents its proteasomal degradation.
evidence: This hypothesis is tested and supported by in vitro proteasome assay data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The proteasome degraded the GST-CTD protein from the C-terminus.
source: Using an anti-GST Ab, the amount of full-length GST-CTD was greatly diminished and a ladder-like pattern of low molecular weight bands was detected, indicating that the proteasome degraded the GST-CTD protein from the C-terminus (Figure 3A, lane 1 and 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the ladder-like pattern of degradation products detected by anti-GST antibody but not by anti-CTD antibody.

claim: The low molecular weight products from GST-CTD degradation were undetectable by WB using an anti-CTD Ab (8WG16).
source: Consistent with this, the low molecular weight products were undetectable by WB using an anti-CTD Ab (8WG16; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The 20S proteasome used was in a latent status with a closed gate and minimal enzymatic activity.
source: Notably, the 20S proteasome used was in a latent status with a closed gate and minimal enzymatic activity (Groll et al., 2000; Forster and Hill, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Groll et al., 2000 and Forster and Hill, 2003.

claim: GST-CTD was capable of activating the 20S proteasome.
source: Thus, GST-CTD, like for example the unstructured protein p21 (Forster and Hill, 2003), was capable of activating the 20S proteasome.
evidence: This is inferred from the degradation of GST-CTD by latent 20S proteasome and comparison to p21.

claim: Low concentrations of SDS render the proteasome gate disordered, leading to proteasome activation.
source: Low concentrations of SDS render the proteasome gate disordered, leading to proteasome activation (Groll et al., 2000; Forster and Hill, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Groll et al., 2000 and Forster and Hill, 2003.

claim: Addition of 0.01% SDS to reaction mixtures increased CTD degradation.
source: Indeed, addition of 0.01% SDS to reaction mixtures increased CTD degradation (Figure 3A, lane 3 and 4).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro proteasome assay data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The proteasome inhibitor MG132 inhibited CTD degradation.
source: In contrast, the proteasome inhibitor MG132 inhibited degradation (Figure 3A, lane 5 and 6).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro proteasome assay data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Recombinant c-Abl phosphorylated GST-CTD, resulting in conversion of a fraction of the GST-CTD to a low-mobility, Tyr1-P isoform.
source: For this, we first used a recombinant c-Abl derivative to phosphorylate GST-CTD. This resulted in conversion of a fraction of the GST-CTD to a low-mobility, Tyr1-P isoform, although the majority remained unphosphorylated (Figure 3C, lane 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is supported by in vitro phosphorylation and Western blot data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The majority of GST-CTD remained unphosphorylated after c-Abl treatment.
source: This resulted in conversion of a fraction of the GST-CTD to a low-mobility, Tyr1-P isoform, although the majority remained unphosphorylated (Figure 3C, lane 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: c-Abl phosphorylates the CTD processively.
source: consistent with the processive phosphorylation by c-Abl observed previously (Duyster et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Duyster et al., 1995.

claim: The Tyr1 hyperphosphorylated GST-CTD was resistant to degradation by the proteasome.
source: Strikingly, the Tyr1 hyperphosphorylated GST-CTD (top panel, upper band, and lower panel) was resistant to degradation (lane 2), while the remaining unphosphorylated GST-CTD (top panel, bottom band) was degraded.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro proteasome assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The remaining unphosphorylated GST-CTD was degraded by the proteasome.
source: Strikingly, the Tyr1 hyperphosphorylated GST-CTD (top panel, upper band, and lower panel) was resistant to degradation (lane 2), while the remaining unphosphorylated GST-CTD (top panel, bottom band) was degraded.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro proteasome assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Addition of 0.01% SDS promoted degradation of unphosphorylated GST-CTD, but the Tyr1-P isoform remained resistant.
source: Addition of 0.01% SDS again promoted degradation of unphosphorylated GST-CTD, but the Tyr1-P isoform remained resistant (lane 3).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro proteasome assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: GST-CTD phosphorylated by the Ser5/Ser7 kinase CDK7 was not protected from degradation.
source: Significantly, GST-CTD phosphorylated by the Ser5/Ser7 kinase CDK7, which converted essentially all of the substrate to the hyperphosphorylated form, was not protected from degradation (lanes 4–6), indicating a specific role of Tyr1-P in preventing proteasomal degradation.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro proteasome assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Tyr1-P has a specific role in preventing proteasomal degradation.
source: Significantly, GST-CTD phosphorylated by the Ser5/Ser7 kinase CDK7, which converted essentially all of the substrate to the hyperphosphorylated form, was not protected from degradation (lanes 4–6), indicating a specific role of Tyr1-P in preventing proteasomal degradation.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of Tyr1-P and Ser5/7-P effects on proteasomal degradation.

claim: Both proteasomal inhibitors epoxomicin and MG132 led to approximately twofold elevated levels of Rpb1-Y1F.
source: Both inhibitors led to approximately twofold elevated levels of Rpb1-Y1F (see Figure 3—figure supplemental 1B for quantification).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3D and quantification in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The proteasome functions in Rpb1-Y1F degradation in vivo.
source: In any event, our data provide evidence that Tyr1, and specifically Tyr1-P, prevents proteasomal degradation of the CTD in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by the effects of proteasome inhibitors on Rpb1-Y1F levels in cells.

claim: Tyr1, and specifically Tyr1-P, prevents proteasomal degradation of the CTD in vitro.
source: In any event, our data provide evidence that Tyr1, and specifically Tyr1-P, prevents proteasomal degradation of the CTD in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro proteasome assay data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Tyr1, and specifically Tyr1-P, prevents proteasomal degradation of the CTD in vivo.
source: In any event, our data provide evidence that Tyr1, and specifically Tyr1-P, prevents proteasomal degradation of the CTD in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by the effects of proteasome inhibitors on Rpb1-Y1F levels in cells.

claim: A total of ∼5 million reads mapping to 3′ regions of genes were generated for each cell type.
source: Cells were treated with tet for 24 hr, and a total of ∼5 million reads mapping to 3′ regions of genes were generated for each cell type (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the sequencing data summary shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: uaRNAs were defined as transcripts that did not overlap any known protein-coding genes and used a poly(A) site within 2 kb from the TSS.
source: uaRNAs were defined as transcripts that did not overlap any known protein-coding genes and used a poly(A) site within 2 kb from the TSS (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is the operational definition used in the analysis.

claim: The number of genes with upregulated uaRNAs was significantly greater than the number of genes with downregulated uaRNAs, by ∼16-fold (p=10−21.5), in 25F+Y cells.
source: Unexpectedly, the number of genes with upregulated uaRNAs was significantly greater than the number of genes with downregulated uaRNAs, by ∼16-fold (p=10−21.5), in 25F+Y cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by 3'READS sequencing data analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: S2A cells showed a fourfold (p=10−6.7) trend of upregulated uaRNAs.
source: S2A and S5A cells showed similar trends but to much lesser extents, fourfold (p=10−6.7) and 5.6-fold (p=10−9.0), respectively, while T4V cells in fact showed a trend in the opposite direction (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by 3'READS sequencing data analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: S5A cells showed a 5.6-fold (p=10−9.0) trend of upregulated uaRNAs.
source: S2A and S5A cells showed similar trends but to much lesser extents, fourfold (p=10−6.7) and 5.6-fold (p=10−9.0), respectively, while T4V cells in fact showed a trend in the opposite direction (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by 3'READS sequencing data analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: T4V cells showed a trend in the opposite direction (downregulated uaRNAs).
source: S2A and S5A cells showed similar trends but to much lesser extents, fourfold (p=10−6.7) and 5.6-fold (p=10−9.0), respectively, while T4V cells in fact showed a trend in the opposite direction (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by 3'READS sequencing data analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: uaRNAs associated with the ARGLU1, METTL14, SH3BP5 and WEE1 genes were upregulated about twofold in two independent 25F+Y cell lines.
source: Using RT-qPCR, we validated several of the uaRNAs (Figure 4C). uaRNAs associated with the ARGLU1, METTL14, SH3BP5 and WEE1 genes were upregulated about twofold in two independent 25F+Y cell lines, consistent with results from RNA-seq (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Levels of RPLP1- and CCNB2-associated uaRNAs were indistinguishable in 26r and 25F+Y cells by both RT-qPCR and RNA-seq methods.
source: Levels of RPLP1- and CCNB2-associated uaRNAs were indistinguishable in 26r and 25F+Y cells by both methods.
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4C and RNA-seq data.

claim: uaRNAs are low-abundant, usually rapidly degraded by the nuclear exosome.
source: uaRNAs are low-abundant, usually rapidly degraded by the nuclear exosome (Preker et al., 2008; Seila et al., 2009; Wei et al., 2011; Ntini et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Protein levels of four exosome subunits were comparable in 26r and 25F+Y cells.
